name.text: Book reference vs object vs class

questiontext.text:
Given the following class and instantiation:

public class Book {
    String title;
    int pages;
    public Book(String t, int p) {
        title = t;
        pages = p;
    }
}

Book b = new Book("Java", 300);

What does b refer to?

answer.text: A reference to a Book object in memory.

feedback.text: Correct! The class is the blueprint, `new Book(...)` creates the object, and `b` holds a reference to that object.

answer.text: A second Book class created from the original class definition.

feedback.text: Classes are not created at runtime with `new`; only objects are.

answer.text: The Book object itself, stored directly inside the variable `b`.

feedback.text: In Java, object variables hold references, not the objects themselves.

answer.text: A method call that returns a newly created Book object.

feedback.text: `new Book(...)` creates the object, but `b` is the variable that refers to it.

answer.text: A copy of the Book class definition.

feedback.text: Each instantiation does not copy the class; it creates one object from the single class blueprint.

questiontext.text:
What is the output of the following code?

public class Counter {
    private int count;
    public Counter(int start) {
        count = start;
    }
    public int getCount() {
        return count;
    }
}

Counter c = new Counter(7);
System.out.println(c.getCount());

feedback.text: The field starts at 0 but the constructor sets it to the argument before getCount() is called.
count is an int, not a reference type, so it can never be null.
Correct! The constructor runs when `new Counter(7)` is executed, setting count to 7.
The constructor argument is 7, not 1.
The code compiles; a constructor with an int parameter is valid.

questiontext.text:
Which of the following declarations will cause a compilation error?

public class Account {
    public Account() { }          // I
    public void Account() { }     // II
    public static Account() { }   // III
}

feedback.text: II is not a constructor: it has a return type, so it is a regular method and compiles.
A method with the same name as the class is allowed as long as it declares a return type.

answer.text: None — all three are valid constructors

feedback.text: III fails to compile: a constructor cannot be marked static.
I is a perfectly valid no-argument constructor.
Correct! Constructors cannot be static. `void Account()` is a legal (if confusingly named) method, not a constructor.

questiontext.text:
What is printed by the following code?

public class Person {
    private String name;
    public Person(String name) {
        name = name;
    }
    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }
}

Person p = new Person("Alice");
System.out.println(p.getName());

feedback.text: Alice is only stored in the parameter, not in the field. The parameter is discarded when the constructor ends.
Correct! The parameter shadows the field, so `name = name` assigns the parameter to itself. The field is never set; use `this.name = name`.
The code compiles; the problem is logical, not syntactic.

answer.text: No output — the program crashes with an exception

feedback.text: The program runs without exceptions; it just prints null.
The empty string is never assigned; the field keeps its default value of null.

questiontext.text:
What is printed by the following code?

public class Printer {
    public void print(int x) { System.out.println("int"); }
    public void print(String s) { System.out.println("String"); }
    public void print(double d) { System.out.println("double"); }
}

Printer p = new Printer();
p.print(5);
p.print(2.5);
p.print("hi");

feedback.text: 2.5 matches the double parameter, not the String one.
The order of calls is print(5), print(2.5), print("hi").
Each call has an exact argument-type match, so overload resolution succeeds.
Correct! Overloading selects the method by argument type: 5 is int, 2.5 is double, and "hi" is String.
The methods print the type names, not the argument values.

questiontext.text:
What is the output of the following code?

public class Entity {
    private int health;
    public Entity() {
        health = 100;
    }
    public void takeDamage(int amount) {
        health = health - amount;
    }
    public int getHealth() {
        return health;
    }
}

Entity e = new Entity();
e.takeDamage(30);
e.takeDamage(20);
System.out.println(e.getHealth());

feedback.text: The takeDamage calls modify the health field; it does not stay at its initial value.
Correct! The constructor sets health to 100, then takeDamage reduces it by 30 and then 20.
Health only reaches 0 if 100 total damage is taken; here only 50 is.
Both damage calls affect the same object's state.
The class and main logic are all valid Java.

questiontext.text:
What happens when the following code is compiled?

public class MathUtils {
    private int version;
    public static int add(int a, int b) {
        return version + a + b;
    }
}

feedback.text: The code does not compile because the static method references a non-static field.

answer.text: Compilation error: methods cannot be declared static.

feedback.text: Static methods are perfectly legal; the problem is accessing the instance field.

answer.text: Compilation error: a static method cannot access an instance field directly.

feedback.text: Correct! `version` is an instance field, so it cannot be referenced from the static method without an object.

answer.text: Runtime exception when add() is called.

feedback.text: The failure happens at compile time, before any code runs.

answer.text: Compiles; version defaults to 0, so add returns a + b.

feedback.text: version is an instance field; even though it would default to 0, the reference to it from a static context does not compile.
